acceptance-qa-batch.summary: Copy each ticket's criteria verbatim and admit only whole backlog items under their own ticket, have a demonstrator write one probe per criterion and a breaker write attack probes for the tickets that earned it, and grade every ticket from the exit codes (0 or 3) of approved probes that code runs alone in checkouts pinned at HEAD and prepared by the operator's commands.
acceptance-qa-batch.preserved: The upstream interface stays: tickets is a backlog path or the text itself, scope is optional, and maxTickets defaults to eight with the excess deferred loudly. The low-effort ingest still reports a runContext, and the order is still demonstrate, then break, with the breaker only on tickets that earned defending. The upstream's install and build step survives as the operator's prepare commands, run before every probe. The breaks-criterion threshold stays, and so does the upstream passed count, which includes pass-pending-manual. Batch 01's separate durable IDs per ticket stay, as demonstrate/<ticket>/plan and break/<ticket>/attacks.
changes: Packaged: workflows/acceptance-qa-batch.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts builds each plan's schema from its ticket's criteria count and fixes the probe exit convention (FailExit = 3) and the criteria and transcription limits. lib/backlog.ts holds admission. lib/checkout.ts holds the backlog read, the dirty-checkout refusal, the pinned base and one prepared probe run. lib/evidence.ts lines answers and runs back up by ticket and position, lib/approval.ts digests and renders each approved list, and lib/policy.ts holds the verdict, status and count rules. Three templates and two fragments (Ticket, Probe) carry the upstream prose.

Code owns the evidence; agents run nothing. The read-only Demonstrator writes one probe program per criterion, or null for one this checkout cannot demonstrate, and the Breaker writes attack probes. A human approves each list (approve-probes, approve-attacks). The subject carries the list, its sorted-key SHA-256, the probe command, the prepare commands and the variable names, and the details show each criterion, claim and probe, with a marker when they do not all fit. Each probe then gets its own fresh worktree pinned at HEAD and one local step there. The step runs the operator's new prepare commands with the full environment, then feeds the probe on stdin to the new required probeCommand with only the probeEnv variables (PATH, HOME, LANG and TMPDIR by default). So a rerun prepares again, and the variable values never enter identity. Exit 0 demonstrates or holds, and exit 3 fails or breaks. A failed prepare, any other exit (Node exits 1 on a crash or a bad import), a timeout, a signal or a command that cannot start is inconclusive, so a broken probe cannot fail a ticket. The approvals add two batch-wide barriers where upstream pipelined tickets. maxAttacks, probeTimeoutMs, prepareTimeoutMs, prepare and probeEnv are new bounded inputs.

Code owns the backlog. It reads the file once, or takes text with a line break or JSON as the backlog itself. It refuses a dirty checkout other than the backlog file (status refused), because every agent reads, and every probe runs at, the pinned commit. It splits the backlog into whole units (list items without marker or checkbox, other lines, JSON strings), each owned by the ticket whose heading, title line or JSON object holds it. A list item titles a ticket only when a separator follows its ID. A ticket is admitted when the backlog names its ID and each criterion is a whole unit of that ticket, or of no ticket when the backlog ties no text to it (a T-number, or an ID named only in prose). So duplicate, invented, reworded, truncated, split and cross-ticket transcriptions are rejected. A list item that nothing copied is listed as unclaimed, whether it sits under a checked ticket, a skipped ticket or none. Under a checked ticket it leaves that ticket pending manual.

The unreachable pass-pending-manual verdict becomes reachable. A ticket with something demonstrated and nothing failed is attacked. It is pending manual when a criterion is undemonstrable or inconclusive, an item is unclaimed, its probes or attacks were declined, or its breaker failed. manual lists what a human still has to check. unverified is new, for a ticket with nothing demonstrated. The output changes shape: tickets[].breaks becomes attacks (severity, probe, outcome broke/held/inconclusive/unrun, run). A criterion carries status, claim, probe and run instead of evidence, and a run's failure names its stage (prepare or probe). deferred lists the deferred tickets instead of counting them. status, dirty, base, runContext, unverified, inconclusive, skipped, rejected, unclaimed and the two digests are new. The status (refused, empty, declined, degraded, limited, complete) reports several things: failed agents, rejected transcriptions, items nothing copied (including those under a skipped ticket), probes without a verdict, deferred tickets and a transcription that reached its limit. maxTickets is now at most 30.

Roles: Ingester is std.claude.ReadOnly at the Copyist tier, matching the upstream's low effort, now spent on a verbatim copy. Demonstrator and Breaker are ReadOnly at the Skeptic tier with high effort. No role edits or holds Bash, so the roster requires no grant beyond read. The probes those roles write run outside grants, behind the approvals, with the operator's privileges and only the probeEnv variables.
acceptance-qa-batch.evaluation: The success fixture asserts these verdicts. QA-1 passes, with a reproduced degrades break (exit 3) and a held criterion-level attack. QA-2 fails on a real exit 3, with one criterion undemonstrable. QA-3 is skipped. It also checks the following. All five probes ran in distinct checkouts under the run's worktree root. Each received only the probeEnv names although the parent process holds others. Both approved digests match a recomputation from the exact lists, and the details and subject name the criteria, claims, prepare commands and variables. It also checks which probe steps ran, that the backlog was handed over whole, that every agent ran without write or shell tools in a run-owned checkout at the pinned commit, and that the checkout is clean at an unchanged HEAD. The modes cover these cases. An uncommitted edit to the backlog is not refused, its text reaches the ingester, and only backlog.md is left modified. A dirty checkout is refused before any call. An ingester that transcribes nothing gives degraded with four unclaimed items. A nested-list backlog whose ingester skips two tickets that have items gives degraded with all three items listed, including a criterion that starts with another ticket's ID. Further modes cover an empty backlog and a dropped criterion (unclaimed, pending manual). Duplicate, truncated, invented and cross-ticket tickets are rejected, including a T1 that copies QA-1's criterion. One mode gives one line of JSON inline under a one-ticket cap. On the agent side, a demonstrator and a breaker each fail. On the probe side, a prepare command installs an ignored package the probes import, which never reaches the source checkout. A failed prepare leaves every probe unrun (inconclusive, naming the command). A reproduced criterion-breaking attack fails its ticket, and its long probes truncate the approval details. A probe and an attack that crash on a bad import are inconclusive, not fail. The rest are a real one-second timeout, a probe command that cannot start, and declined probe and attack lists. Scratch mutants of the verdict, status, admission, backlog-exclusion, prepare, environment and inline rules each fail the mode meant to catch them (seven last round, nine this round). F3 kills the owner after a probe step ran in its pinned checkout and before its checkpoint; the resume prepares and reruns the probe and pays for no completed call. Limits: prepare reruns in every probe's checkout, so an install costs one run per probe. The limited status for a transcription that reaches 100 tickets has no mode. Admission understands Markdown headings, title lines, list items and JSON. So a non-criterion bullet under a ticket is reported unclaimed, a table-based backlog is rejected, and a ticket the backlog ties to no text gets no ownership check beyond not copying another ticket's items. An exit code proves only what the probe tests, so a tautological probe still passes; the human approval is the only guard against that. No model quality is measured.

acceptance-qa-deep.summary: Pin the delivered work, uncommitted and untracked files included, as a snapshot commit; decompose the criteria into binary sub-checks; check each criterion in a checkout of that snapshot and have a second harness challenge each pass; then compute every status and the gate verdict in code.
acceptance-qa-deep.preserved: Kept from the upstream: the decomposition into binary sub-checks, the implied criteria (flagged and checked like stated ones), the per-criterion check-then-challenge pipeline with no barrier, the challenge only on passes, the fail-spirit downgrade, the done / done-pending-manual / not-done / no-criteria verdict, and the stakeholder summary with its code-written fallback when the summary agent fails. Kept from Batch 01: the rule that evidence comes from the code and never from PR text, and the rule that cannot-verify is a manual case, never a pass.
changes: Packaged: workflows/acceptance-qa-deep.ts is control flow only. lib/snapshot.ts pins the delivered work in one local step (a temporary index, write-tree, then commit-tree, so the source index, files and branches are untouched) and lists and diffs it. The workflow's 'snapshot' worktree handle then pins that commit under the run's refs at once and hosts the commands that lib/checks.ts runs. lib/policy.ts holds the status, downgrade and verdict rules and the fallback summary. Four templates under prompts/, with Delivered and Commands fragments, restore the upstream guidance.

Code owns the target. The free-text target becomes base (HEAD for a dirty tree, otherwise the latest commit's parent, as upstream) plus paths, and the checker and challenger read a runtime-owned checkout of the snapshot instead of the live tree. 'Run it where cheap' becomes operator-selected checkCommands: a red suite is a completed result that keeps its output, and a signal or timeout settles. The checker and the challenger both receive the results. criteria is text, or criteriaFile that code reads, instead of guessing that a value without a newline is a path.

The checker answers holds, fails or cannot-verify for each sub-check (the schema requires one answer per sub-check), and code derives pass, partial, fail or cannot-verify. The pipeline is a settled ctx.map (version criteria/2) that runs three criteria at a time; Batch 01 ran eight, and the upstream had no limit of its own. A failed checker leaves its criterion unchecked, and a failed challenge, settled inside its item, leaves the pass unchallenged; both count as pending manual and make the status degraded. Upstream, a failed checker returned null and graded as cannot-verify, only a stage that threw dropped its item, and an unchallenged pass counted as clean. A failed narrator settles too: code writes the upstream's fallback paragraph and summarySource says code.

No silent caps. maxCriteria caps the checklist, skipped criteria are reported, and status says complete, degraded, limited or no-criteria. The decomposition schema allows 60 stated criteria, 30 implied criteria and 12 sub-checks per criterion. Decompose.md states these limits, tells the decomposer to keep every stated criterion rather than merge, and to split a criterion that needs more sub-checks; the upstream had no limits. Roles: the Decomposer is the Planner tier with no tools, the Checker the Skeptic tier at high effort and read-only, the Narrator the Copyist tier (the upstream's low-effort summary), and the Challenger std.codex.ReadOnly at high effort, so a different harness from the checker's judges each pass.

Interface: the input's target becomes base and paths, and criteria becomes criteria or criteriaFile (exactly one); checkCommands, maxCriteria and maxPatchBytes are new. The output adds status, head, snapshot, base, uncommitted, files, patchTruncated, commands, pendingManual and summarySource. Each criteria entry carries implied, kind and per-sub-check checks, in place of an '(implied) ' prefix and one evidence string.
acceptance-qa-deep.evaluation: In the fixture, greet.mjs is improved in the working tree but not committed, beside an untracked test. The source checkout holds the same files, so the command passing proves nothing by itself; instead, the record shows that the test command, the checkers and the challenger all ran in checkouts based on the snapshot. The fixture checker also reads greet.mjs from its own checkout, so a checker handed HEAD's stub would fail. Every mode asserts that the source status, index, HEAD and branches are unchanged; the only refs added are refs/quiet-choir pins, and the reported snapshot is pinned even when nothing is checked. Modes cover: a dishonest challenge (fail-spirit, not-done); a benchmark-only sub-check (cannot-verify, done-pending-manual, never challenged); a partial criterion beside it (not-done with a must-fix, the manual case kept); a failed checker, challenger and narrator (unchecked, unchallenged, a code-written summary, degraded); a nonzero exit and a SIGKILLed command, with base, paths and criteriaFile set, where the failing criterion is not challenged; the criteria cap (limited); a committed tree (base is the parent); and an empty decomposition. Seven mutations each fail the self-check: counting cannot-verify as a pass, dropping it from pending, collapsing partial into fail, challenging non-passes, running commands in the source checkout, withholding commands from the challenger, and basing the snapshot handle on HEAD. F3 does not apply because the gate writes nothing. The fixture decomposer, checker and challenger are rule tables, not models, so nothing here measures how well a real checker or challenger judges intent.

api-migration.summary: Search the pinned base for the old API in code, group the call sites into disjoint file groups, approve the exact plan, migrate each group in its own worktree in bounded waves with code-checked receipts, and publish only an integration that the operator's commands and the leftover search verified, after at most one three-cluster repair round.
api-migration.preserved: The upstream's discover-then-shard shape, disjoint file groups (a module and its inseparable test together), batchSize waves with the early stop when a whole wave is blocked, migrated/partial/blocked accounting with blockers, the single global verification, one repair round over at most three failure clusters followed by a re-verify, and its prompt guidance (indirect uses such as re-exports and mocks, match the surrounding style, leave an unmigratable site on the old API) all remain. Batch 01's empty-group strictness (#65) becomes a schema rule: a discovered group has at least one file.
changes: Packaged: workflows/api-migration.ts is control flow only; contracts.ts holds the discovery, migration, triage, repair and output schemas, lib/policy.ts the scope, coalescing, coverage, digest, receipt and status rules, lib/checks.ts the Git listings, the old-API search and one verification pass, lib/stages.ts the two writer stages, and four templates under prompts/ (with a shared FROM/TO/notes fragment) the prose.

Upstream deliberately ran its editors in one tree, trusting that discovery's groups were disjoint. Here each migrator and repairer gets a runtime-owned worktree pinned to the base or the integration, and code refuses a receipt that changes a file outside its approved set or adds, deletes or renames one; groups that share a file are coalesced and untracked paths reported as stray, so disjointness is enforced rather than assumed. Nothing is written before ctx.approve over the plan and its digest, and every writer receives the approved plan JSON verbatim.

The agent verifier becomes code: the required verifyCommands (operator argv) run on the integrated tree with nonzero exits recorded as results, so the full red output survives, and the optional searchTerms let code find the old API at the base (hits that discovery neither grouped nor excused are reported as unassigned) and in files reported fully migrated (leftovers). A text-only Triager clusters the failures, at most three Repairers fix clusters in parallel, a conflicting repair is dropped, and the second pass runs only when a repair landed.

Waves are settled maps: a failed migrator keeps its group on the old API as failed and a refused receipt as refused; groups past maxGroups are deferred and those after an all-blocked wave unattempted. The status names each outcome (nothing-to-migrate, declined, nothing-migrated, verification-failed, publish-failed, unverified-publish, partial, migrated). Publication merges only the agents' receipts, never the verification checkout's artifacts, and code compares the published tree with the verified one.

Roles: the Discoverer (std.claude.ReadOnly, Scribe tier) reads, the Triager (std.claude.Text, Scribe tier) has no tools, and the Migrator and Repairer (std.claude.Edit, Mechanic tier) write only in worktrees, so under --require-grants a launch grants --grant Migrator --grant Repairer. The upstream sets no effort on any call.
api-migration.evaluation: The success fixture finds four files by code search, approves two groups, checks that the two migrators got distinct worktrees and the approved plan verbatim against its digest, requires the verification command (red while a file mentions legacyFormat) to pass, and publishes exactly a.mjs and b.mjs without the command's artifact. Modes cover a declined plan, a discoverer that missed both call sites (reported unassigned), an all-blocked first wave that leaves the second unattempted, a failed and an out-of-bounds migrator (partial publication, with coalescing and a stray path), a code-found leftover that one repair fixes while a second, conflicting repair is dropped, a red and a self-killed command with an unchanged repair, and an operator commit after verification, reported as unverified-publish. F3 kills the first migrator invoked, after its edit. The fixtures prove the gating, ownership and accounting, not that a real discoverer finds every call site or that a migration is semantically right.

bug-hunt.summary: Rotate read-only finder panels until two dry rounds, deduplicate candidates, and settle a skeptic panel per candidate with std.patterns.tolerantPanel, keeping undecided outcomes and failure counts.
bug-hunt.preserved: Batch 02's convergence rule, dedup against everything seen, majority arithmetic with missing seats, logical-call cap and explicit failed/skipped/undecided counts remain.
changes: Both panels are std.patterns.tolerantPanel calls filled from the roster (a PanelTeam with Finder, then Skeptic). Each member's outcome is journaled, so a failed vote stays failed on resume; the version option names the prompt and schema, which the settled map's fingerprint does not show. Leaf IDs become round/<r>/finders/<i>/answer and round/<r>/skeptics/<k>/<seat>/answer.
The upstream's full lens descriptions and the majority, key and severity rules live in lib/policy.ts; findings are sorted most severe first, as upstream returned them.
Roles: Finder is the Scribe tier; Skeptic is the Skeptic tier at the upstream's high effort. Skeptic items carry the candidate, so its panel's fingerprint covers what is judged.
bug-hunt.evaluation: Fixtures inject a failing skeptic seat (undecided), failing finders (no dry convergence), a three-call cap and a reported-cost stop with a higher-cap resume, as in Batch 02. Fixture cost is simulated usage, not billing; concurrent admissions can overshoot a cost threshold.

codebase-atlas.summary: Pin the commit and its tracked files in code, match a core-first, capped survey against them, deep-read each subsystem into a card in a settled map, assemble the atlas around a synthesized overview in code, and merge one critique's grouped repairs before a guarded write.
codebase-atlas.preserved: The upstream's survey-then-fan-out, core-first ordering with the default eight-subsystem cap and its skipped list, the card fields with gotchas as the prized one, the synthesis barrier, the four-part document (what this is, a Mermaid system map of dependsOn edges, one section per subsystem with gotchas prominent, start here with three files) and the single completeness-critic repair round of at most three remain. So do Batch 01's out and maxSubsystems inputs and the docs/atlas.md default.
changes: Packaged: workflows/codebase-atlas.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the survey, card and critique schemas and a synthesis schema whose start-here paths are an enum of verified key files. lib/git.ts holds the commit, status and ls-tree commands, lib/policy.ts the path matching, cap, coverage, gap grouping and status, and lib/atlas.ts the document and its Mermaid map. The prose is five templates under prompts/ with Card and Evidence fragments.

Code owns the document. The system map's edges are exactly the cards' dependsOn, and a dependency on a skipped or unread subsystem is a dashed not-deep-read node rather than an external service. Each section renders its gotchas first, and the Synthesizer, which has no tools, writes only the overview and start-here. The upstream's write-atlas and merge-repairs agents, which wrote the file and then rewrote it in place, become one ctx.writeFile of the merged cards. That write is exclusive by default. With the new replace input it is a compare-and-swap against the digest read before any agent ran, and an existing out without replace is refused before any agent is paid.

Code owns the facts. The survey sees a layout built from git ls-tree. Its loosely spelled paths are normalized and matched to tracked files, and a subsystem that matches none is listed as unmatched. Top-level areas no subsystem covers are handed to the critic. A key file that is not tracked is dropped and reported. The atlas names its commit and says whether tracked files were dirty.

Every failure is accounted for. Readers and repairs are settled maps: a failed reader leaves its subsystem unread, and a failed repair changes nothing. The critic is a settled call that yields 'critic unavailable', as upstream. Its gaps are grouped by section, so two complaints about one card make one repair. maxRepairs (default 3, the upstream constant) caps those groups and reports the rest as unrepaired. complete is derived from an empty gap list. The status reads complete, repaired (gaps repaired but not re-reviewed), limited, degraded, empty or refused.

Roles: the Surveyor and the Synthesizer are the Copyist tier (the upstream's low effort), and the Reader is the Scribe tier for both deep reads and repairs. The Critic is a read-only Codex role at high effort, so an independent harness audits what the Claude readers wrote. No role edits.

dead-code-sweep.summary: Sweep three modalities as a tolerant panel, give every candidate a settled skeptic that keeps it unless it is cleared, and delete an approved, digested list in an isolated worktree that code verifies before publishing.
dead-code-sweep.preserved: The upstream's three sweeps (exports never imported, unreachable from entry points, stale by history), the per-candidate falsification with its default to keep, the report-only default and the single remover that sees how deletions interact all remain; Batch 01's step IDs for the sweeps, the cross-check and the removal stay.
changes: Packaged: workflows/dead-code-sweep.ts is control flow only; contracts.ts holds the input (apply needs a verification command), candidate, verdict and output schemas, lib/policy.ts the merge, cap and list digest, lib/checks.ts the base commit and verification commands, and three templates under prompts/ the prose.

The sweeps are std.patterns.tolerantPanel: a failed sweep is counted in failedSweeps instead of failing the run. The cross-check is a settled ctx.map, so a skeptic that fails keeps its candidate as unchecked-and-kept instead of aborting or deleting.

Removal is gated by ctx.approve over the exact list and its digest, runs as the Edit-tier Remover in a worktree pinned to the base commit, is ownership-checked to the listed files, integrated, verified by the operator's commands in a fresh verification worktree, and only then merged into the checkout.
A cap on candidates is reported (unchecked) rather than silent, and the status names each outcome: nothing-dead, report, declined, verification-failed or applied.
dead-code-sweep.evaluation: The success fixture finds an unimported legacy.mjs from two modalities, approves it, deletes it in the remover's worktree and requires the verification command (which fails while the file exists) to pass before the checkout changes; other calls must be read-only. Modes cover report-only, a failing skeptic (the candidate is kept) and a red verification (the checkout is untouched). F3 kills the remover after its edit and before its response is recorded. The fixtures prove the gating and accounting, not that a real sweep finds dead code.

deep-code-review.summary: Pin merge-base..head in code, give each of up to five dimensions a read-only reviewer over a snapshot of the head, deduplicate in code, and report only findings that a settled default-to-refuted skeptic could not refute, with every failure and cap accounted for.
deep-code-review.preserved: The upstream's five dimension charters remain, each saying what its reviewer must ignore. So do the barrier before deduplication (a cross-dimension duplicate costs one verifier, not two), keeping the more severe copy, one skeptic per finding that refutes when uncertain and may move the severity either way, the report written from survivors only, and the code-written sentence when nothing survives. Batch 01's scope, review, verify and report stages keep their order, and the dimensions input keeps its name.
changes: Packaged: workflows/deep-code-review.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the range input and the typed finding, verdict and output schemas that feature-factory can consume per module; lib/git.ts pins the range and cuts the patch; lib/policy.ts holds the line budget, deduplication, verification slots, verdict rule, read-only receipt check and status; four templates and three fragments under prompts/ hold the prose.

Code owns the scope. The plain-language target becomes base (default HEAD~1), head (default HEAD) and paths. Git pins merge-base(base, head)..head, lists the changed files with numstat, and hands reviewers the patch inside <patch> tags under a changed-line budget; the Scoper only summarizes it. Reviewers and skeptics read per-call snapshots of the pinned head (worktree: { base: { commit } }), and code refuses a snapshot that changed. Uncommitted changes are therefore no longer reviewable, which was the upstream default.

Reviewers and skeptics run as settled ctx.map calls. A failed reviewer becomes unreviewedDimensions, and a failed skeptic leaves its finding unverified, where upstream silently dropped it. Deduplication compares lines fewer than five apart instead of floor(line / 5) buckets, never merges line-less findings by file alone, and records every reporting dimension and the titles it absorbed.

Caps are reported, never silent: files past maxChangedLines are unreviewedFiles, and findings past maxFindings (ranked by severity, then by how many dimensions raised them) are unchecked. status says nothing-to-review, complete, degraded or limited. Roles: Scoper and Reporter are std.claude.Text at the Copyist tier (the upstream's low effort), Reviewer is ReadOnly at Scribe, and Skeptic is ReadOnly at the Skeptic tier with high effort.
deep-code-review.evaluation: The success fixture commits three helpers (two with real defects), a generated file, and a guide outside paths. Reviewers get only src/. Code merges the correctness and performance copies of the lastN defect; a skeptic refutes one claim and raises another's severity. Every reviewer and skeptic runs outside the checkout, and the checkout, HEAD and refs are left as found apart from one base pin per snapshot call, all at the head. Modes cover a failed reviewer, a failed skeptic, both caps, all findings refuted (code-written report, no Reporter call), no findings, nothing in scope (no agent call), and an unknown base that fails with a named error. The fixtures prove the accounting, the code-owned scoping and the read-only placement, not that real reviewers find real defects. Uncommitted changes and pathological long-line patches under the line budget are outside them.

dependency-upgrade.summary: Code finds the package's manifest lines and usage files. A web researcher reads the changelog while an analyst maps the usage, and a human approves one joined plan, which an upgrader applies in an isolated worktree. A code-run loop then installs, verifies, triages and fixes disjoint files: it either publishes a green, in-plan tree as one commit or reports the root causes that still fail.
dependency-upgrade.preserved: The upstream's parallel research and impact analysis still meet at one justified barrier. The high-effort plan keeps its trivial and reconsider rules, and the single applier, the three-fixer cap on root-cause clusters and the fix-forward guidance all remain. The maxFixRounds bound keeps its honest report of what still fails when the loop does not converge, and the not-attempted, unstable and upgraded outcomes remain. The upstream labels research, impact, plan and apply become the step IDs. A failed triage ends the loop unstable, as the upstream's unavailable verifier did.
changes: Packaged: workflows/dependency-upgrade.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the input and every agent schema, and the lib/ modules hold the rest. lib/git.ts has the clean check, the base, the usage search, the manifest evidence and the tree diff. lib/verify.ts runs each round's install and verification commands. lib/policy.ts has the caps, the coverage rule, the digest and the approval preview, the ownership check, the cluster assignment and the left-failing report. lib/stages.ts holds the fixer. Six templates under prompts/ (three fragments) restore the upstream's guidance. In the roster, the Researcher (web tools only), the Analyst and the Triager (read-only) are at the Scribe tier, and the tool-less Planner is at the Planner tier (the upstream's high effort). The Upgrader and the Fixer, the only writers, are at the Mechanic tier.

Code owns the facts. git grep at the pinned base finds the files that name the package, and the analyst must classify each one as usage or unrelated; files it leaves unclassified, or past maxUsageFiles, are reported. git grep also finds the manifest and lockfile lines both analysts read, so the Researcher needs only WebSearch and WebFetch. The upstream verifier agent becomes code: the operator's installCommand, then each verifyCommand, run in a fresh checkout of the integrated commit. Exit 0 is green, and truncated output is recorded but is not a failure. Nonzero exits are kept as data (okExitCodes 'any'), so the Triager reads a 4 KiB tail of each red command's output.

Writes are approved and contained. A human approves the hashed plan and its file list before the Upgrader runs in a worktree pinned to the base. Each writer's receipt is checked against the plan's files plus the manifests. Clusters get disjoint files, so up to three Fixers run in parallel worktrees of the integrated commit and their changes cannot conflict. Code checks that HEAD is still the base after the approval, before every integration and before publishing, and returns base-moved otherwise. It publishes one squash commit only when the last round is green and the integration changes nothing outside the plan. Because the verification commands run in the published checkout, an install's lockfile is published; a verify command's writes to allowed files are published too, and an unignored file they write outside the plan refuses publication.

The loop: every fix round is verified, which removes the unverified last repair that the Batch 01 note describes. rounds counts verifications, at most maxFixRounds + 1. maxFixRounds 0 now means 'verify once, never fix' (the upstream's `|| 3` turned 0 into 3), and maxFixRounds is capped at 5. A red round with no fix round left is still triaged, but only for the report: its clusters are marked not-attempted. remaining then lists the last red round's root causes, or its failing commands when the triage named none. These are strings instead of the upstream verifier's {description, files} objects; the files are in the last round. A round whose fixers change nothing stops early.

Semantics: a failed analysis or plan now fails the run, which can be resumed, instead of returning aborted. A failed triage is a settled call: it ends the loop unstable, and the round records triage 'failed'. New statuses: declined, refused, unchanged and base-moved. verifyCommands is a new required input; installCommand and manifests are new optional ones.

design-tournament.summary: Generate four designs under forced philosophies, have an independent panel score the anonymized proposals with each seat seeing its own order, tally the rubric, the winner, ties and dissent in code, and synthesize on the winner with a recorded graft or rejection for every losing idea.
design-tournament.preserved: The four proposer identities, the fixed A–D anonymization, independent judges scoring every proposal on the four-axis rubric, the arithmetic tally, the abort below two proposals and the six-point dissent threshold carry over from the upstream and Batch 01. The inputs brief, context, judges and out keep their names. winner, scoreboard, design, grafts and dissent stay in the output, with grafts and dissent reshaped.
changes: Packaged: workflows/design-tournament.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the Proposal schema, plus Scorecard and Synthesis schemas built per call from the surviving letters and the idea IDs. lib/policy.ts has the letters, seat rotation, tally, tie-break, dissent, graft ledger and existing-out rule, and lib/render.ts the tournament record that code appends to the document. Three templates plus Proposal and Material fragments hold the prose.

Proposers and judges run as settled maps (onError: 'return') keyed by philosophy and seat, and each call gets one retry on a schema or transient failure. A member that still fails is journaled and reported in failedProposals or failedJudges with status degraded, not silently filtered out. Dissent and idea credits name the real seat; the upstream indexed the filtered list. A scorecard must score each presented letter exactly once on 1–10 axes. A proposal must have a title of at most 160 characters, 1–16 components and 1–10 each of tradeoffs and risks. Anything else counts as a failed member once its retry fails. judges is bounded to 1–7; the upstream had no bound, and 0 meant 3. A panel with no surviving scorecard is status unjudged, where the upstream picked a winner from zeros.

Output reshaped. grafts is now a per-idea ledger (id such as B1, from as a letter, title, idea, judges, decision, reason), replacing the upstream's per-loser { from: <title>, judgesLiked }. dissent is always an array of { judge, total, avg, rationale }; the upstream returned a string when there was no dissent or the run aborted. Each idea is a judge-named best idea from a losing proposal, merged across judges by text, ignoring case and whitespace. The Synthesizer returns its markdown plus one decision per ID, and its panel count is the scorecards that counted. Code records undecided ideas and appends the scoreboard with per-axis means, the ledger and the dissent. The dissent now reaches the synthesizer's prompt; the upstream computed it only after synthesis.

out is created exclusively, as a file or, with publication: 'commit', as a managed commit. The upstream overwrote it. Here an existing out refuses the run (status refused) before any agent call, and one that appears mid-run still fails the final write. Each seat sees the proposals in its own rotation. Ties go to mean fitness, then letter, and are reported as tiedWith. crossHarness seats every second judge on a read-only Codex CodexJudge at high effort.

Roles: Proposer is ReadOnly at the Scribe tier, Judge is ReadOnly at the Skeptic tier with high effort, and Synthesizer is Text at the Planner tier with ReadOnly's spend and time limits. No role writes. A parent that composes this package under --require-grants (prd-to-spec) maps Proposer, Judge and Synthesizer to a Claude ReadOnly ceiling and CodexJudge to a Codex ReadOnly ceiling, even with crossHarness off, because delegation checks every declared entry when the child starts.
design-tournament.evaluation: The success fixture checks: the scoreboard arithmetic and per-axis means; the dissenting seat; merged idea IDs and their decisions; a byte-exact exclusive write with the code record in the document; judge prompts free of philosophy names and identities, in rotations ABCD/BCDA/CDAB; and the tool lists (proposers and judges read only, the synthesizer has no tools). Eight modes cover: two failed proposers (degraded; judges see only A and C); the abort below two proposals with no further calls; every judge failing (unjudged, no synthesis, no file); one of four judges failing (degraded, dissent and idea credits keep seats 2–4, and the synthesizer is told 3 judges counted); an existing out refused with no agent call and a clean checkout; an undecided graft; a tie broken on fitness; and a four-seat cross-harness panel published as a commit on a clean checkout. The one-judge mode catches dissent numbered by surviving position, a status that ignores failed judges, and a synthesizer count taken from the input; all three mutants pass every other mode. F3 kills after the write and before its checkpoint. Not checked: an out that appears between the check and the write, scores and graft decisions (still agent judgments), and whether a grafted idea actually entered the design. The six-point dissent threshold is upstream policy, not calibrated.

docs-drift-audit.summary: Pin HEAD, list the docs in code for a tool-less librarian to rank, and run one barrier-free pipeline per doc that extracts quoted claims, anchors them in code, checks them in a snapshot of the base with operator-chosen evidence and patches drift in an isolated worktree; a patch is published only after a human approves it, its verifyCommands pass when given, and HEAD is still the base.
docs-drift-audit.preserved: The upstream's four phases and its pipeline shape remain. The inventory gives each doc an audience and a priority, takes high first, and reports the maxDocs cap. Each doc is decomposed into the seven claim kinds, with check hints and quotes. One batched checker per doc answers true, drifted or unverifiable and suggests replacement text. An opt-in fix runs per drifted doc and does not wait for the other docs. The report-only default, the input names paths, fix and maxDocs, and Batch 01's per-doc stage order all stay.
changes: Packaged: workflows/docs-drift-audit.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the input, the path-constrained classification, the claim, positional check and fix schemas, and the output. lib/git.ts has the base pin, the cleanliness check for fix runs, the listing with sizes, the root-relative heading outlines, the HEAD checks and the patch. lib/policy.ts has the ranking, quote anchoring, prompt fencing, receipt judgment, pipeline collation, the run and fix statuses, and the approval preview. lib/checks.ts has the evidence and verification runners, and four templates under prompts/ hold the prose.

Code owns what is audited. HEAD is pinned. paths changes from a free-form string to a list of 1 to 20 Git pathspecs, listed with git grep -I at the base. The default (Markdown, MDX, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc and README files anywhere) no longer covers other files under docs/. Changelogs are always excluded; docs over maxDocBytes, past maxInventory or with unusual names are reported. The Librarian and the Extractor are std.claude.Text and work from the paths, headings and doc text that code extracted. A claim whose quote is not in the doc (ignoring whitespace, backticks and asterisks) is dropped as unanchored, and that degrades the run. Results pair with claims by position, and each doc's pipeline is one item of a settled ctx.map (version doc/3).

The read-only Checker (Scribe tier) works in a fresh checkout of the base, entered at the repository root. The upstream's "run --help" becomes evidenceCommands: an argv, or {argv, okExitCodes} for a tool whose help exits nonzero. Code runs each command once in another checkout of the base, at the run's directory within it. That checkout holds committed files only, so a report-only run ignores the state of the source checkout. A spawn failure, timeout, signal or unaccepted exit (an ignored build that is absent, say) degrades the run. The checkers see that outcome marked failed and are told to judge from the source. Each output sits in an <evidence> block that names the JSON argv and cannot be closed early.

The Fixer (std.claude.Edit, Copyist tier, the upstream's low effort) patches one doc in a worktree at the base, entered at the root. Code refuses a change to any other file and a rename, and measures resolved, unresolved and collateral claims by quote. ctx.merge starts from the checkout's live HEAD, so code integrates the accepted changes only while HEAD is still the base. The integration is one squash commit, and code checks that its parent is the base. Code then runs verifyCommands, which pass on exit 0. With no verifyCommands, the approval asks to publish an unverified patch. A human approves the exact patch; the question carries its SHA-256, its size and, past 15,000 bytes, a marked preview cut on a character boundary. Code publishes the patch to the checkout only if HEAD is still the base after the approval. A fix run refuses any tracked change or untracked file before any agent call, by the same rule the checkout merge applies. totals.fixed counts resolved claims in published docs.

The output is reshaped. doc becomes path, with audience, priority and bytes. The claims count becomes a results array holding each claim's quote, status, reality and suggested text; the drifted list is that array filtered. The per-doc fixed count becomes a fix record, and skipped strings become {doc, reason}. listed (every matched doc: audited, failed or skipped), unclassified, evidence (with ok) and failed are added. status reports no-docs, complete, limited (a cap or a path rule skipped docs) or degraded (a failed doc pipeline or evidence command, a doc the librarian left unclassified, a capped claim list, an unanchored claim, or a drifted doc whose fix is missing from the patch). fix.status reports not-requested, no-drift, no-change, refused, failed, verification-failed, declined, moved (before integration, or while the approval waited), publish-failed or applied. fix.omitted names the drifted docs whose fix is not in the patch. The upstream's default inventory of CLI --help templates as docs is dropped. A help template is audited only when paths names it, and evidenceCommands treat --help output as evidence, never as a doc.
docs-drift-audit.evaluation:
In the success fixture, docs/config.md ranks above README.md and CHANGELOG.md is never listed. The extractor gets each doc's committed text and the checker its anchored claims in order. Both checkers work in checkouts of the base and get the --help output. README.md is patched in the fixer's worktree, and the verification command, which fails while --yes remains, passes. The human sees the whole patch, which is a squash commit on the base touching README.md only. The digest of the published diff equals the approved one. Only the fixer has Write; the librarian and the extractor have no tools. Modes cover these cases:
- report-only, where a quote without its backticks still anchors, and a dirty checkout that a report-only run ignores
- a declined patch with collateral
- red verification, and loud verification (exit 0 with truncated output)
- a fixer that also edits cli.mjs, and one that renames the doc (both refused; degraded)
- two drifted docs, where one fixer is refused and the other doc is published (applied, degraded, the refused doc in omitted)
- a failed fixer (degraded, fix failed)
- a HEAD that moves while the fixer works (moved before integration: no verification, no question, nothing published)
- a HEAD that moves while the approval waits (moved after approval of a patch that holds only the fix)
- an untracked file that appears during the run (publish-failed)
- a patch over the preview limit (marked cut)
- a failed checker (degraded; the other doc is still fixed, and the approval says unverified)
- an evidence command whose ignored build is absent from the fresh checkout: exit 1, degraded, marked failed for the checkers, and the fix still publishes
- a spawn failure, an accepted nonzero exit, a librarian skip and a capped claim list
- paraphrased quotes, so nothing is checked (degraded)
- the size cap, unanchored claims and an unclassified doc (degraded)
- the inventory cap with a backslash-named doc (limited, both reported)
- every doc over the cap (limited), and no docs
- a run started in docs/ (root-relative paths and outlines, agents at the root, evidence at the run's position)
- tracked or untracked changes, which refuse a fix run before any call

F3 kills the fixer after its edit and before its response is recorded. The squash-parent check is reached only by a move in the instant after the first HEAD check, or by a resume after a crash between the two. A mutation run that removes the first check confirms that it catches the moved mode alone. A conflicting commit landing in that instant still fails the run. Quote anchoring and quote-based fix accounting are heuristics: a paraphrased quote is dropped, and a fix that keeps the quote counts as unresolved. The fixture's degraded rule admits only such unresolved claims. The fixtures prove the pipeline and its accounting, not that a real checker finds drift. Evidence and verification commands run in fresh checkouts, so they see only committed files, unless the package declares worktrees.setup, which an operator cannot do. Under --require-grants, a report-only run still needs --grant Fixer.

feature-factory.summary: Run prd-decompose as a typed child, have a planner group its tickets into disjoint modules under a call cap that a human approves, build the foundations in order and the features in parallel in worktrees, review each built module with a deep-code-review child, repair confirmed findings in isolation, and publish only an integration the operator's commands verify.
feature-factory.preserved: The upstream's five phases (decompose, plan modules, implement, review, stabilize) remain, with prd-decompose and deep-code-review as the children whose structured returns are the composition interface. So do foundations built one after another before parallel feature builders, explicit disjoint file areas per module, a planner that places every ticket or defers it with a reason, the builder's honest done/partial/blocked report, one review per implemented module, repairs that fix confirmed findings without re-judging them, maxModules with loud deferral, and an output of backlog, modules, deferred tickets and verification. Batch 01's real child ports become the Batch 03 packages, declared as typed children with stable frame IDs (decompose, reviews/<n>/review).
changes: Packaged: workflows/feature-factory.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the input (verifyCommands required), the plan schema built from the backlog, the builder and fixer replies and the output. The plan schema's refinement in lib/plan.ts refuses overlapping areas, a dropped or doubly placed ticket and a dependency that would build later. lib/plan.ts also holds the call bounds, digest, build order and ownership rule; lib/stages.ts the two isolated writer stages; lib/policy.ts the outcome bookkeeping, delegation maps and status; and lib/checks.ts the clean-checkout, base, inventory and verification commands. Three templates and two shared fragments hold the prose.

Composition: prd-decompose and deep-code-review are the sibling packages' workflows, imported and declared as children. Under --require-grants, options.profiles maps all eight child entries onto one read-only Reader ceiling, so --grant Builder --grant Fixer is the whole launch. Each review child is a settled ctx.map item over the module's own snapshot commit against the commit it built on (deep-code-review reviews committed ranges only), so a failed review is counted rather than fatal. The upstream's codebase hint is now prd-decompose's directory input.

Isolation replaces the shared checkout. Each builder works in a worktree pinned to the last foundation that landed, and features start from the foundation tip. Its receipt is checked against its areas, so any path outside them, or a rename, is refused. A module whose dependency did not land is skipped. The fixer works on the module's snapshot. Code integrates the accepted changes, runs the operator's verifyCommands on a fresh verification tree, and fast-forwards a clean checkout only when they pass. The roles have no shell, so the builders' narrow checks and the upstream's 'find the commands' verifier become those operator commands.

A human approves the exact plan before any builder runs: the digest covers the text every builder receives. The upstream's low-budget guard after the foundations becomes maxCalls: each stage is admitted at its upper bound (the children's included) before planning, which caps how many modules the planner may use. The upstream's notes string is replaced by a status of applied, limited, degraded, verification-failed, nothing-built, declined or no-tickets. It shows caps, deferrals, failed or refused builds, failed reviews and unrepaired findings.
feature-factory.evaluation: The success fixture decomposes a three-requirement PRD through the child and approves a plan with one foundation and two features; every builder prompt carries the approved plan verbatim, matching its digest. It checks that both features build on the foundation's snapshot in distinct worktrees, that each review child reads only its own module, and that the fixer corrects hello's confirmed typo. The verification command fails without that fix and must pass before the checkout fast-forwards; all other calls must be read-only. Modes cover a declined plan, a red verification (the integration stays on a run-owned ref), a failed feature builder, an overreaching feature builder, a blocked foundation whose dependents are skipped, a failed review child, an empty backlog, the call cap deferring a module, a plan refused by its schema and retried, and a requireGrants run with only the two writer grants. F3 kills the foundation builder after its edit. A launch missing the Fixer grant was checked only in a scratch run, because a mode cannot assert a refusal that leaves no run record. The fixtures prove composition, gating and accounting with inert replies, not that real agents decompose, build or review well.

feedback-synthesis.summary: Parse a feedback corpus into numbered items in code, fix the theme vocabulary on an evenly spread sample, tag disjoint shards in a settled map, count, rank and check quotes in code, and deep-dive the top themes into a report that code renders around the reporter's prose.
feedback-synthesis.preserved: The upstream's order stays: calibrate, then shard. So do its fixed vocabulary with an other catch-all, at most two themes per item, severe counts (churn threat, data loss, blocked workflow, safety), the items-plus-four-times-severe rank, emergent patterns, the deepDives cap (default 4) and the report's shape: at most three summary bullets, a theme table, a section per dive, a long tail and emergent patterns. Batch 01's focus and deepDives inputs keep their names; its source becomes sources.
changes: Packaged: workflows/feedback-synthesis.ts holds only the control flow. lib/corpus.ts reads each source as a durable snapshot and parses it (lines, blocks, jsonl or RFC 4180 csv) into F1…Fn with path:line refs, then draws the even sample and cuts the disjoint shards. lib/policy.ts aggregates, ranks, checks quotes and derives the accounting and status. lib/report.ts renders the report. Four templates and three fragments under prompts/ hold the prose.

The upstream inventory agent is gone, and coverage is no longer the taggers' word. Code numbers every item and gives each tagger its shard verbatim; the tagger schema admits only that shard's IDs and the vocabulary's keys. Every item ends up in one of four states: tagged, off-focus, untagged (its shard failed or the answer left it out; listed by ID), or unsharded (past maxShards). The upstream dropped unknown theme keys without a word and believed each tagger's itemsRead.

Quotes are checked. A tagger's or a diver's quote counts only if it is a verbatim excerpt (whitespace-normalized; a cut marker is ignored) of the item it names. A tagger's quote must also come from an item it tagged with that theme. Every other quote is dropped and counted. The reporter writes only the summary, long-tail and emergent prose. Code renders the coverage line, the theme table, each dive with its quotes and path:line refs, and a not-covered list.

Taggers and divers run as settled maps (onError: 'return', with version tag/1 and dive/1). A failed shard leaves its items untagged and a failed dive is reported; both degrade the status. The other theme is never deep-dived. All four roles are std.claude.Text with no tools: the Tagger is the Copyist tier (upstream low), the Calibrator and Diver the Scribe tier, and the Reporter the Planner tier (upstream high).

New bounded inputs replace implicit choices: format, textField and fields (columns the operator selects, so an id or email column never reaches a prompt), severityWeight (the upstream's 4), sampleSize, shardSize, maxShards and diveItems. The status is complete, limited (shard cap hit, or an item cut at 1,500 characters), degraded or empty.
feedback-synthesis.evaluation: The success fixture parses a twelve-row CSV that contains a quoted comma, doubled quotes and a two-line record. It checks: the even sample, which leaves out F6 and F12; three disjoint shards covering exactly F1–F12; the repeated vocabulary key dropped and other added; the severity-weighted ranking, in which one severe export report outranks three mild other items; four dives that skip other and read severe items first; verbatim quotes with path:line refs in the code-rendered report; the source's SHA-256; no tool on any call; no id column in any prompt; and an untouched repository. Seven modes cover a failed tagger, a focus filter, a sloppy tagger and diver (an omitted item, a duplicate tag, two paraphrased quotes), a failed dive, the shard cap, an item cut at the character cap, and a blank source next to a missing one. F3 does not apply (read-only) and F5 does not apply (no questions). The fixtures prove the accounting, parsing and quote checks, not tagging quality: whether the vocabulary stays consistent across shards still depends on the calibrator and the taggers.

flaky-test-hunt.summary: Sweep three blind evidence sources, stress-run each screened suspect with the operator's single-test argv so code computes every flake rate and verdict, diagnose only flakes measured at one commit, and publish an approved fix only after code checks its files, re-stresses and verifies it on the measured commit, and finds the checkout still there.
flaky-test-hunt.preserved: The upstream's three blind evidence sources stay, with the merge by file and test, the corroboration ranking and the cap on stress runs. So do the flaky / stable / always-fails / could-not-run verdicts, although could-not-run is narrower (see the changes). Diagnosis is still only for empirical flakes, with its closed mechanism taxonomy and its rule that retries fix only genuinely external dependencies. The report-only default behind fix stays, as do the five re-stress runs after a fix (now fixRuns). Batch 01's input names (scope, runs, maxSuspects, fix) and output names (confirmed, cleared, skipped) also stay, though several output shapes change (see the changes).
changes: Packaged: workflows/flaky-test-hunt.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the schemas: the input (a required testCommand argv with {file} and {test} placeholders, plus testFiles, passPattern, fixRuns, verifyCommands, runTimeoutMs and historyDepth), the suspect, stress, diagnosis, plan and output. lib/policy.ts holds the pure rules: the history facts, merge, test-file screen, cap, $-safe argv substitution, pass pattern, verdict arithmetic, plan, digest, marked approval preview, and the ownership and coverage checks. lib/git.ts holds the clean-checkout step and the Git reads, and lib/stress.ts the settled stress loop and verification. Three templates under prompts/ share a read-only fragment and hold the prose.

Code owns every fact, verdict and file it runs. A local step reads the last historyDepth commits and hands the history sweeper the commits that mention a flake, with their test-file diffs, and the test-file churn, counting what it does not list; with neither, that sweep is skipped and named in noEvidence. The CI sweeper gets an artifact inventory that code lists. Corroboration counts modalities, so a sweep that names a test twice counts once, where the upstream counted every mention. The operator's argv runs a file a sweeper chose, so a suspect must name a tracked file that the operator's testFiles globs list, and a test name that is not an option, or it is rejected unrun. The screen uses positive pathspecs only, because git ls-files ignores an exclude pathspec when the positive ones share a directory. Each stress iteration is a settled ctx.exec (okExitCodes 'any'), and suspects run one at a time in the checkout, all of them before any diagnosis: the upstream's per-suspect stress-then-diagnose pipeline becomes a barrier, because code reads the residue and HEAD after the last run. The upstream's stress agent and its agent-chosen test command are gone.

Output shapes and one verdict change from Batch 01. skipped lists the capped suspects instead of counting them. cleared, broken (always-fails) and unrunnable hold the measured runs. confirmed nests its stress and a nullable diagnosis, the notes string is gone, and fixSummary keeps the fixer's own account. could-not-run now means only that the command did not start, or that a passing exit lacked passPattern. A test that needs a live service, which the upstream called could-not-run, fails every run and lands in broken, because code cannot tell a missing service from a real failure. Nor can code see that a runner ran no test, and some runners (node --test, mocha --grep, go test -run) exit 0 when no test matches the name. So stable means only that every run exited 0, and each stress keeps the output tail of its first passing run. An optional passPattern, whose {test} becomes the escaped name, turns such an exit into could-not-run.

Sweeps and diagnoses are versioned settled maps rather than tolerantPanel. A failed sweep is named in failedSweeps, and a failed diagnosis leaves its flake confirmed but undiagnosed. A diagnosis must give a confidence and the files its fix changes. A flake diagnosed 'unknown' is listed in unplanned and never fixed, where the upstream applied every proposed fix. With fix: true, a human approves the exact plan and its digest: each fix's measured failures and runs, its mechanism, confidence, explanation and proposed fix, and exactly the files its diagnosis named, so a fix placed in the code under test does not also license an edit to the test. One Surgeon-tier Fixer then works in a worktree pinned to the measured commit. Code refuses a change outside the approved files, and every rename, which the fix prompt rules out because it deletes its source (refused). It also stops a change that leaves an approved fix's files untouched (incomplete). Receipt paths are compared with plan paths joined to the run directory's repository prefix, so a run from a monorepo subdirectory publishes. Code then re-stresses each fixed test fixRuns times in a fresh tree of the fixer's snapshot (the measured commit plus the fix), runs verifyCommands in another fresh tree, and merges only the fixer's change into the checkout.

The status names each outcome: sweeps-failed, no-suspects, all-rejected, unmeasured (no suspect could run), no-flakes, report, no-plan, declined, refused, incomplete, fix-failed, moved or fixed. A clean-checkout local step throws on a dirty checkout and returns HEAD. It runs at the start, again before the approval, because stress runs can leave residue, and again before the publish; because it checks the checkout live, cleaning and resuming works. HEAD is also read after the stress runs on every path, report-only included. moved.during says when HEAD left the measured commit. 'stress' means later runs may have measured the new HEAD, so the rates stand as recorded and nothing is diagnosed. 'diagnosis' means nobody is asked. 'fix' covers the approval, the fixer and the re-stress: the held fix stays unpublished, because ctx.merge into the checkout would rebase it onto the new HEAD, and fixCommit names the snapshot on its run ref. Residue also reaches the diagnostician as a fact.
flaky-test-hunt.evaluation: The success fixture measures 3 failures in 8 runs for a cache test keyed on its run's step ID, so retries and replays keep the rate. It clears an always-passing test, separates an always-failing one, and sends only the measured flake to a diagnostician. It rejects a suspect in an untracked file and a tracked migration script that must never run. It checks that the code-read history (with the retry commit's diff), the CI inventory, the measured runs and the argv as JSON reached their agents. It also checks three things about the approval and the fix: the approval subject holds the measurement, the diagnosis and exactly the diagnosed files; its plan and digest are what the fixer received; and the fixer's tree was pinned to the measured commit. The fix is published only after five clean re-stress runs and a verification command on the measured commit plus the fix, and only while the checkout is still at that commit. Every other call is read-only. Modes cover report-only and a declined approval whose long plan is cut in the details with a marker. They cover a failed diagnosis and an 'unknown' mechanism, both of which end no-plan, and two flakes of which only one is explained (fixed, the other unplanned and the output degraded). Others cover a fix that still flakes, a red verification and a fixer that changes nothing (incomplete). Three fixers are refused: one that edits an unapproved file, one that edits the test where the diagnosis named the code under test, and one that moves an unapproved file onto an approved path. Re-stress residue is kept out of verification and the publish. Further modes cover one or all sweeps failing, empty sweeps, all suspects rejected, a history with no evidence, operator testFiles globs and the corroboration-ranked cap. Others cover suspects that all share tests/ (an option-like test name rejected), a lone suspect whose runs time out (never diagnosed) and a runner that exits 0 on no match (caught by passPattern, read as stable without it). The rest cover a command that cannot start (unmeasured), a run from a monorepo subdirectory that publishes, a dirty start and stress residue. A teammate's commit that breaks the clock test lands in one of three places. During the stress it ends moved with nothing diagnosed, even report-only. During the diagnosis it ends moved before anyone is asked. While the approval waits, the fix is still pinned, re-stressed and verified on the measured base, and held unpublished. That last mode relies on a module-level note, because answer() receives neither mode nor env. F3 kills the fixer after its edit and before its response is recorded. Nine mutations were run this round, and each fails the mode that guards it. The fixtures prove the measurement, accounting and gating. They do not prove that a real sweep finds real flakes, that eight runs detect a low-rate flake, or that five runs prove one gone. Nor do they prove that the default globs or a given passPattern fit a real runner, or that a fresh tree has the dependencies a real suite needs. A commit that lands between the last HEAD read and the merge's preparation would still be published onto. A checkout that moves and returns during the stress runs reads as unmoved.

incident-investigation.summary: Pin the Git window, collect facts in four hypothesis-free domains with read-only Codex roles, falsify each competing hypothesis, and derive the report's confidence from the verdicts in code.
incident-investigation.preserved: The pinned window, read-only Codex roles and the three code-owned clean-repository checks (before, after collection, after the report) remain.
changes: The upstream's structure returns now that prose and contracts live outside the control flow: four collector charters (diffs, logs, config, deps) in one template, facts with source, timestamp and oddity, hypotheses with falsifiable predictions, and one falsifier per hypothesis with a falsified, survives or untestable verdict.

Confidence is structural and computed in lib/policy.ts, as upstream: one survivor with a rival falsified is high, a lone survivor medium, several split, none none. A falsifier that failed leaves its hypothesis unchallenged, which caps a lone survivor at medium.

Collectors and falsifiers are settled maps (onError: 'return'), restoring the upstream's tolerance of a failed member with explicit accounting: uncollected domains and null verdicts are in the output. It uses a settled map rather than tolerantPanel, whose answers dropped the item a verdict must keep when this port was written; its outcomes now keep each item.
Roles: Collector, Theorist, Falsifier and Reporter are std.codex.ReadOnly; the last three keep the upstream's high effort.
incident-investigation.evaluation: The dirty-collector fixture still fails at the code status check, now after four collectors. A failed-falsifier fixture shows the unchallenged hypothesis and the capped confidence. The success fixture gets high confidence from one survivor and one falsified rival. Ignored files, external writes and transient changes restored before status remain outside the check; Codex sandbox enforcement is covered by the harness tests.

prd-decompose.summary: Read the PRD once in code, extract anchored work items through five settled lenses, and merge them into numbered, dependency-ordered tickets that carry their items' anchors. A backwards coverage critic then alternates with anchor-checked patch repairs until an audit passes or maxRepairs runs out, and code schedules the tickets and writes the backlog.
prd-decompose.preserved: The upstream's five lenses keep their charters and anti-charters. The barrier before the merge stays, and so does the merger's rule that ticket identity is judged by reading, not by key. The lane and size enums, acceptance criteria, PRD anchors, dependency edges and pooled open questions all stay. The reverse-direction critic still reports missing, under-specified and wrong gaps, and there is one repair round by default. The output still carries tickets, sequencing, coverage and openQuestions, which is what feature-factory reads, and Batch 01's single repair still bounds the default run.
changes: Packaged: workflows/prd-decompose.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts builds the merge, coverage and repair schemas from the ids each may cite, and checks a repair's anchors against the PRD. lib/sources.ts reads the PRD and lists the codebase, and lib/anchors.ts matches quotes. lib/policy.ts collects items, carries anchors onto tickets, applies repair patches, schedules the tickets and decides the status. lib/render.ts writes the document. The prose is four templates and four fragments under prompts/.

Code owns the facts. The PRD is read once: an input containing a newline is the PRD text, and anything else is a repository path. codebase becomes a directory whose tracked files code lists for the lenses. A directory with no tracked file, such as a prose hint, is refused before any call. Code looks up each lens item's prdAnchor in the PRD and never merges an item it cannot find. A merged ticket carries its source items' anchors instead of the merger's copies, and a repair whose anchor is not in the PRD is refused. Code computes the dependency waves and the critical path. It renders the markdown and creates the file exclusively, or publishes it as a managed commit, where upstream used a low-effort writer agent.

Failures are accounted for. The lenses are a settled ctx.map, so a failed lens is named in failedLenses and degrades the status, even when no item survives. When every lens fails the status is unread, not empty, so a consumer cannot mistake an outage for a PRD with nothing to build. The critic and the repairer settle too, giving unaudited and gaps-remain. A merge failure other than a schema error now fails the run, and resume retries it, where upstream returned an empty 'Merge failed' backlog. The merge schema requires T1..Tn in dependency order and allows one schema retry. Code decides coverage from the gap list, not from a boolean the critic reports.

The repairer returns a patch that code applies, so a repair cannot silently drop tickets. The patch holds added tickets, complete amendments (title, description, criteria, estimate and anchors) and an optional revised sequencing. It cannot change a ticket's lane or dependencies, or the open questions. Every repair is audited again: maxRepairs (default 1) bounds the loop, and covered means the final backlog passed an audit. A default run is nine calls, the same as upstream with out set, because the second audit replaces the writer agent.

Roles narrow to std.claude.Text. LensReader is the Scribe tier, Merger the Planner tier (the upstream's high-effort merge), Critic the Skeptic tier at high effort, and Repairer the Scribe tier. Merger, Critic and Repairer borrow ReadOnly's spend and time limits.
prd-decompose.evaluation: The success fixture checks the PRD receipt and that every lens gets the PRD text and the tracked-file list. It checks an anchor accepted through an ellipsis and different case, an XL item split to L, and tickets T1–T5 with their sources, carried anchors, waves and a 10-day critical path. The repair must receive the PRD, add T5, retitle and amend only the retry ticket, and revise the sequencing. The second audit must read the repaired backlog, a byte-checked docs/backlog.md must be the only new file, and no call has a tool. Modes cover: a failed lens, degraded although the critic is satisfied; every lens failing, unread with no merge and nothing written; one failed lens with the rest unanchored, degraded rather than empty; maxRepairs 0, gaps-remain with nothing written; and inline PRD text whose quotes are all unanchored, empty with no merge and deduplicated questions. They also cover a failed critic with a one-file listing cap and commit publication (unaudited, the cap reported, a clean checkout), and a repairer that misquotes the PRD on both attempts, whose patch is refused (gaps-remain). The rest are refusals: an existing out refused after nine calls, a prose codebase refused before any call, and a failed merge that fails the run. F3 kills the run after the write and before its checkpoint. F1 and F2 hit the first lens, a settled member, so they show tolerance of a failed lens, not a resume after a failed run. An anchor check proves a quote exists, not that the ticket implements it. The critic's gap quotes are not checked, and ticket quality and the critic's judgment are not measured.

prd-to-spec.summary: Read the PRD and list the codebase in code, ground once, draft five technical lenses as a settled map, settle a load-bearing top decision with the design-tournament package's workflow as a settled inline child, and merge, audit twice and repair once into a spec whose headings and decision IDs code checks.
prd-to-spec.preserved: The upstream's greenfield switch, the grounding map, the five lens charters, contested decisions ranked by stakes with only a load-bearing top decision earning a tournament, the merger's nine-section structure and self-decided Decisions section, the two independent audits (implementability, and fidelity in both directions), the single repair round that defers owner questions to Open questions, and the open questions read back from the final spec all remain; Batch 01's ordinary imported tournament child stays a typed child, now with a recorded settled outcome.
changes: Packaged: workflows/prd-to-spec.ts is control flow only; contracts.ts holds the lens, audit and spec schemas (SpecDocument refuses a merged or repaired spec without the nine level-2 headings in order or with a contested decision ID missing from Decisions, and the schema retry asks again), lib/sources.ts the PRD read, codebase listing and out precheck, lib/policy.ts the decision merge and ranking, the tournament record, the audit records, the delegation map and the status, lib/spec.ts the fence-aware heading and open-question rules, and seven templates under prompts/ the prose, two of which (Brief, Context) render the child's input.

Code owns the facts the upstream asked agents for: the PRD is read once (inline text or a repository file, bounded by maxPrdBytes), the tracked files are listed for the grounder, an existing out refuses the run before any call, the same decision raised by two lenses is merged by text into one ID with both lenses' options, and the spec is written by exclusive create or std.exec.committedArtifact instead of a low-effort write agent.

The tournament is ../../design-tournament.quiet-choir's workflow declared in children and run with ctx.workflow(..., { profiles, onError: 'return' }): a failed child is a durable branch (the merger decides D1 itself), a child that completes without a winner adopts nothing, and the output records the child's status, winner and whether its design was adopted. judges and crossHarness pass through; Reader and CodexReader ceilings map the child's four entries under --require-grants, CodexReader even when crossHarness is off.

Fan-outs account for failure: lenses and audits are settled maps keyed by name, a failed lens or auditor is listed (failedLenses, audits[].completed), a failed repair keeps the merged spec, and status says verified, repaired (the revision is not audited again, as upstream), degraded, undrafted or refused. Audit verdicts are derived in code from the gap lists; the upstream's passed flag and verification string become a structured verification record.

Roles narrow: Grounder and LensWriter are std.claude.ReadOnly at the Scribe tier; Merger (Planner tier), Auditor (Skeptic tier at high effort) and Repairer (Scribe tier) have no tools and borrow ReadOnly's spend and time limits; nothing edits, so a --require-grants launch needs no grant.
prd-to-spec.evaluation: The success fixture runs ground, five lenses, the eight-call tournament, merge, two audits and a repair (18 calls), asserting the merged and ranked decision ledger (D1 from two lenses with three options), the brief and context the child received, the adopted design with the child's tournament record in the merge prompt, the PRD only in the fidelity audit, the repaired spec's open questions, byte-exact publication and read-only or tool-less calls. Modes cover a greenfield inline PRD with no load-bearing decision (no tournament, verified, nothing written), a failed lens and auditor, a failed and an aborted tournament child, a failed repair, a schema-refused merge retried, every lens failing, an existing out, and requireGrants with no grant, a Codex judge seat and commit publication. F3 kills after the spec write and before its checkpoint. The fixtures prove the control flow, accounting and code-owned checks, not the quality of a real spec, and a refused merge is retried with the same prompt.

project-bootstrap.summary: Detect the stack, approve one hashed plan, apply each concern in its own worktree, and integrate only after code-run verification.
project-bootstrap.preserved: Batch 02's canonical plan digest, durable approval before any write, disjoint file ownership checked on each receipt, per-concern worktrees, settled verification commands and publication only on success all remain, with the same step IDs.
changes: Packaged: the digest, ownership and preview rules are pure functions in lib/plan.ts, the Git baseline and verification loop are lib/checks.ts, and the three prompts are templates; the Apply template still ends with the approved plan JSON, which the fixture parses back and compares with the approved subject.
The upstream's stack override returns as an optional input, and the Surveyor reports the stack it chose, which the output records.

Roles: Surveyor (Scribe tier) and Planner (the Planner tier, the upstream's high-effort plan) read; only the Setter (std.claude.Edit with the Mechanic tier) writes, always inside a runtime-owned worktree, so under --require-grants a launch grants --grant Setter alone.
project-bootstrap.evaluation: Fixtures check the approved digest against a sorted-key hash of the approved subject, two isolated setter checkouts, the plan in each setter prompt, a real exit 7 and a self-SIGKILLed verify command settled as verification-failed, and a resume that pays nothing again. Commands are approved operator-privileged programs; argv is not a sandbox, and worktrees isolate repository edits only.

refactor-campaign.summary: Survey and rank refactoring targets and pin each one with a characterization net. Code runs every net green on the current code, alone and then together. After a human approves the hashed goal and plan, it refactors one target at a time behind every net, keeping only changes that leave the nets alone, keep every net and verify command green, and that a reviewer judges structural.
refactor-campaign.preserved: From the upstream: the survey by measurable pressure, with evidence and testability, and the ranking of payoff against risk, which names a specific refactoring. Also the maxTargets cap, the net-first gate (no green net, no refactor), and net, then refactor, then verify for each target. The report-only default stays, the nets stay in place after apply, and the output keeps the refactored, netOnly and skipped groups and a summary line. From Batch 01: the survey-then-rank order and the green-net gate. Three things Batch 01 flagged have changed: agents running the tests, report-only writing tests into the checkout, and concurrent edits to one checkout.
