changes: Packaged: workflows/refactor-campaign.ts holds only the sequence. lib/stages.ts holds the two per-target stages as team-typed patterns, each run under a map item or ctx.scope: pinNet with a NetTeam writer, and refactorTarget with a refactorer and a reviewer. lib/policy.ts holds the rules for net acceptance, collisions, the digest, bounds, duplicates and the summary. lib/checks.ts holds the settled commands, the bounded git excerpts the agents see, the clean-checkout and moved-HEAD checks, and the merge-refusal rule. Five templates under prompts/ hold the prose and share one behavior-preservation fragment.

Code owns every test verdict, and the survey no longer reports a test command. Each net runs as the operator's testCommand argv with the net's path appended, in a probe checkout of the writer's snapshot, and the exit status decides. The command runs with okExitCodes 'any', so a repair prompt gets the last 4 KiB of each output stream, not the 1024-character tail of a settled failure. A net is one new test file plus its declared supportFiles. The writer's receipt must add exactly those files, and the net must name at least one behavior. A red net is rewritten up to netRounds - 1 times, each time in a fresh checkout of the base, from its exit status, its output and its previous files. truncatedRepairFiles counts the files shown only in part, and a superseded file is never published. The agents' netStillGreen claims are gone.

Report-only no longer writes to the checkout. The green nets go into a run-owned commit, which the summary names, and every net and verify command must pass on that commit; otherwise the status is baseline-red, before any approval or refactor is paid for. Apply needs verifyCommands. A human approves the hashed goal and plan, and every refactorer receives that text verbatim. Refactors run one at a time, each on the last kept result. Code discards a refactor that touches any net's files (both sides of a rename, via git diff --no-renames), turns a net or a verify command red, is declined or left empty by the refactorer, or is judged behavioral by the reviewer. The reviewer sees every touched path and is told that an edit to an existing test counts as behavioral. This is the upstream's net-held-reverted, now decided by code.

Publication. An apply run first refuses a dirty checkout, as the result dirty-checkout rather than a throw, because a resume would replay the recorded status. Code integrates the nets and the kept refactors, runs every net and verify command on that integration, and publishes it with ctx.merge only if HEAD is still the run's base. Every merge settles. If HEAD has moved (checked before the approval, after a refused merge and before the publish), the status is checkout-moved, and commit names what is left to merge. That is the nets commit, the last kept result when the integration conflicts with the new commit, or the verified integration. A merge refused while HEAD is unmoved, such as a dirty checkout at publish, ends merge-refused. refusal names the step and Git's reason.

Interface and accounting: maxTargets is capped at 8. netOnly[].planned is now refactoring, and behaviorsPinned is the list rather than its count. Plan entries add netFile and supportFiles, skipped[] adds refactoring and failed, and refactored[] adds commit, files, review and reviewedWhole. A reviewer veto or a red verify lands in netOnly (the net was kept), where the upstream put a failed verify in skipped. The status is dirty-checkout, no-targets, no-nets, baseline-red, report, declined, verification-failed, checkout-moved, merge-refused, nets-only or applied. failedNets, failedCalls, truncatedRepairFiles, duplicateTargets, reviewedWhole and deferred count what was lost. The approval details say when they show only part of the plan. Roles: the Surveyor (Scribe tier, read-only) and the Ranker (Planner tier, no tools). The NetWriter and Refactorer are Surgeon tier, matching the upstream's high effort, and edit only in worktrees. The Reviewer is Skeptic tier at high effort, with no tools.

release-gate.summary: Pin the range since the previous tag on a checkout that is exactly HEAD, run the operator's tests and evidence commands there in code, assess five dimensions with settled read-only assessors in pinned checkouts, confirm each reported blocker on Codex, and let the gatekeeper choose only among the decisions a code-owned gate rule allows.
release-gate.preserved: The upstream's six dimensions keep their charters and status vocabulary (pass, concern, blocker, not-applicable, cannot-check). The policy and blockOn inputs keep the upstream defaults. Each blocker an assessor reports still faces one adversarial confirmer, which may clear it or downgrade it. The structural pre-verdict from confirmed blockers remains. So do the gatekeeper's forwardable rationale and conditions, and the code fallback decision when the gatekeeper fails, which Batch 01 dropped. The result keeps its decision, blockers, warnings, dimensions, rationale and conditions.
changes: Packaged: workflows/release-gate.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the schemas and DecisionFor(allowed), which narrows the gatekeeper's decision enum to what the gate rule allows. lib/git.ts pins the range and reads where HEAD is, and lib/checks.ts runs the operator's commands. lib/policy.ts holds the excerpt budget, the refusal reasons, how a command ended, the rows, the gate rule, the fallback, the read-only receipt check and the status. Three templates and three fragments under prompts/ carry the upstream charters. Roles: Assessor is std.claude.ReadOnly at the Skeptic tier with the upstream's high effort. Confirmer is std.codex.ReadOnly at high effort, so a blocker faces an independent harness. Gatekeeper is the Planner tier with no tools. Each assessor and confirmer works in its own unchanged worktree of the pinned commit, which leaves a run-owned ref under refs/quiet-choir/ until workflow rm --refs. A reader whose receipt shows a changed file counts as failed.

Code now produces the evidence that the upstream asked agents to gather. range becomes since and tagPattern. The default since is the nearest matching tag that is not HEAD's own, so a tagged candidate is gated against the previous release. An explicit since must be an ancestor of HEAD, or the gate refuses. The new testCommands and evidenceCommands are operator argv, and a dimension's evidence output reaches only that dimension. commandTimeoutMs bounds each command. maxRangeChars is one budget for the log and patch excerpts in every reader prompt, and the log takes at most a quarter of it. Before any command runs, the checkout must be exactly HEAD: an uncommitted change or an untracked, non-ignored file refuses. After the commands, a moved HEAD (another commit or another branch) or a rewritten tracked file refuses. Test artifacts are allowed, but one that is not git-ignored refuses the next gate run in that checkout. Ignored files, such as dependencies, remain a boundary. A dirty checkout, an empty range, a missing tag or a bad since gives a refused, fail-closed no-go.

The tests dimension is the operator's testCommands, settled in code with okExitCodes 'any' so the failing output survives. A command that fails on some run (a nonzero exit or a crash by signal) and never passes is a blocker, even next to a command that could not start. A command that passes on its rerun is a flaky concern. A command that could not start, or that timed out and then neither passed nor failed, is cannot-check and degrades the gate. A finding quotes the end of a failed run's output. testCommands is empty by default. tests is then cannot-check, which rules out go under the default blockOn. Code's own test blocker faces no confirmer, so a red test that the range did not cause stays a no-go, where the upstream's confirmer could have downgraded it.

The pre-verdict is now a veto rather than advice. A blocker on a blockOn dimension allows only no-go. Any other blocker, or a hard-block dimension nobody could verify, rules out go. With no blocker and every hard-block dimension verified, the gatekeeper chooses only between go and conditional-go, so concerns alone never produce a no-go. The upstream prompt said the same, but its gatekeeper could ignore it. blockOn is an enum of the six dimensions, so it matches exactly instead of by substring. A confirmer's concern downgrades a blocker to a warning, and its not-a-problem clears it. A cleared blocker no longer appears in warnings; upstream, every unconfirmed blocker did.

Assessors and confirmers are settled ctx.map calls keyed by dimension, and every role gets one retry on schema, transient and process failures. A failed assessor leaves its dimension unassessed, which degrades the gate, and a hard-block dimension is then also unverified. A failed confirmer keeps its blocker standing as unconfirmed, with the cause as its reasoning. When the gatekeeper also fails its retry, code takes the first allowed decision, marked decidedBy code, which degrades the gate. That fallback adds one condition per blocker and one per unverified hard-block dimension. Upstream, a blocker whose confirmer failed dropped out of both blockers and warnings, and the fallback was silent. The result adds status (complete; limited for a clipped excerpt; degraded; refused), reason, decidedBy, allowed, the pinned since/start/end/manifest, unverified, the tests and evidence rows, and the log and patch sizes.
release-gate.evaluation: The success fixture tags the baseline v1.0.0. It checks the default range, the range line in every reader prompt and the Decide prompt's rule and hard-block lines. It checks a test command that passes only on the gated tree, and that the security command's output reaches only that dimension. Every reader works in its own clean checkout of HEAD. The run leaves six run-owned pins of HEAD and no new branch, and the checkout is untouched. Thirty-two modes cover the branches. Tests: red, crashed by SIGKILL, red next to an unstartable command, flaky, fail-then-timeout, unrunnable, and no testCommands. Gate rule: a non-default blockOn (checked in the gatekeeper's prompt too), a confirmer's clear and downgrade, and three blockers with disagreeing confirmers under an operator policy, which checks that each verdict and each case stays with its own dimension. Range: an explicit ancestor since, a since off HEAD's history, an empty range, and a clipped log and patch that split one budget. Failures: unstartable and timed-out evidence commands, failed hard-block and non-hard assessors, a failed confirmer (two calls each), and a gatekeeper that fails its retry. With tests skipped, the fallback adds unverified conditions; with tests passing, the fallback is the only degradation. Readers: an assessor and a confirmer that write to their checkouts. Checkout: an allowed test artifact, a tagged HEAD, and commands that commit or switch branch. Seven refusals happen before any agent runs. A fixture reply that throws now fails its contract instead of quietly becoming an unassessed dimension. In scratch, 37 mutants each failed at least one mode, and the unmutated copy passed all 33 contracts. The mutants include the nine that the last review found surviving and new ones for the HEAD checks and the excerpt budget. F1 and F2 recover inside the retry without degrading; F3 does not apply to a read-only gate. The fixtures pin the gate rule, how it counts failed roles and commands, and the lines each role is handed. They do not show that an assessor's judgment is right. They do not exercise a real Codex sandbox, ignored dependencies that a suite reads, a command that moves HEAD and moves it back, or a multi-megabyte release diff.

release-notes.summary: Pin the commit manifest in code, summarize disjoint slices from their patches, draft for a named audience, and fact-check in both directions with std.patterns.reviewRevise before code publishes the bytes.
release-notes.preserved: Batch 02's code-owned manifest, disjoint slices, set-arithmetic coverage, exclusive or committed publication and bounded fact-check/revision remain, with the same step IDs for the Git commands, slices and write.
changes: Packaged: workflows/release-notes.ts is control flow only; contracts.ts holds the slice schema derived from each slice's own SHAs, lib/git.ts the window, patch and log commands, and four templates under prompts/ the prose.

The upstream's audience input returns, and so does its guidance: diff-not-message summaries, breaking changes first with migration notes, the bidirectional fact-check (claims to commits, commits to claims, emphasis). Summaries carry userVisible and a migration note; the output lists breaking changes and deprecations again.

The fact-check loop is std.patterns.reviewRevise with a ReviewTeam of Drafter (actor) and FactChecker (critic): up to maxRevisions + 1 checks as fact-check/review/<n>, a revision after each rejection except the last. The fact-checker also receives a code-owned git log of the range, so it is not limited to the summaries it checks.
Roles narrow: Summarizer is the Copyist tier at the upstream's low effort, Drafter has no tools (std.claude.Text), FactChecker is the Skeptic tier at high effort.
release-notes.evaluation: The success fixture asserts the manifest equals rev-list, full coverage, factChecked and byte-exact publication, and every agent call records its template. reviewRevise returned { approved, draft } only when this port was written, so the output carries factChecked instead of Batch 02's concern list, and the critic's feedback stays in the run record (workflow inspect). reviewRevise now also returns that feedback, which a later revision could report. Coverage proves commit representation, not factual accuracy. F3 kills after the file write and before its checkpoint, as in Batch 02.

requirements-to-prd.summary: Check the PRD's destination before anything runs, read the material in code, extract quoted findings through four settled lenses whose quotes code checks, draft a PRD traced to them from the first 40 conflicts and unknowns, attack it with three settled critics and revise it once, with optional durable question rounds that redo the PRD with the answers and keep the earlier PRD when a redo drafts none.
requirements-to-prd.preserved: From the upstream: the four lenses and three critic charters with their anti-charters, the stated/implied/inferred tiers, conflicts presented as decisions, and one revision whose unresolvable fixes become open questions. Answers still count as stated requirements, and the empty-extraction result (the unknowns as open questions) and the optional PRD file stay. The upstream's re-run with answers (its checkpoint pattern) is still the default, and a question round asks the same open questions the checkpoint returns, an empty extraction's unknowns included. From Batch 01: text that spans lines is material, and a single line is a path.
changes: Packaged: workflows/requirements-to-prd.ts is control flow only. contracts.ts holds the input, extraction, critique and PRD schemas and the caps all four prompts state (the PRD reply is built from the finding ids it may cite and the caps of its call). lib/out.ts checks out (and, for a commit, a clean checkout) and publishes it, lib/material.ts does the durable reads, lib/policy.ts the quote check, pooling, listing for the writer, assumptions rule, revision caps, issue order, a round's open questions, status and summary, lib/render.ts the document and the question's details, and four templates under prompts/ (with two fragments) carry the upstream's charters.

Code owns what the upstream left to agents and to a regular expression. It reads the material once and numbers the findings. A stated or implied finding stays inferred unless its quote is found in the material or the answers: the parts between ellipses must occur in order and hold at least three words. Every inferred finding a requirement relies on gets an assumption. The writer is given the first 40 pooled conflicts and unknowns, conflicts first, within a cap of 60 open questions; the rest are reported in unlisted and make the status limited. A revision's caps rise by one open question and one assumption per issue. Code renders the PRD from the writer's structured sections, so assumptions and open questions (now with their consequences) are data rather than markdown parsed back.

Failures are counted. Lenses and critics are settled maps with one schema retry. The final round's failures are named in failedLenses and failedCritics, and an earlier round's in its asked entry (status, failedLenses, failedCritics). Issues reach the writer most severe first. A failed revision keeps the draft (unrevised), as does a critique from which every critic failed (unrevised, not critiqued), and a critique with no issues skips the revision. An answered round whose redo drafts no PRD keeps the earlier PRD and makes the status degraded; failedRedo names that round, its failed lenses and the answers the PRD lacks. The draft has one schema retry only, so a draft reply that is invalid twice, or a draft call that fails once, fails the run.

Interface: input is inline text that spans lines, one repository-relative file, or a list of up to 20, bounded together by maxMaterialBytes (over it, the run fails before any agent runs). A directory, an absolute or home path, or several paths in one string no longer work. Blank material with answers is still read. out is checked before any agent runs. An existing file is refused (status refused, nothing read or paid) unless replace names its sha256, and that is how a re-run with answers now redoes a previous PRD. publication 'commit' creates out as a managed commit: it cannot replace, and a checkout Git reports as dirty, untracked files included, is refused up front rather than at the merge. questionRounds (default 0) asks the open questions, or an empty extraction's unknowns, as a durable question and redoes the PRD under round/<n>. The prd markdown is now rendered by code, with requirements numbered R1.. and N1.., a Traceability appendix of the findings and a closing provenance line with the status and summary. New outputs: status (complete, limited, degraded, unrevised, empty or refused), material, rounds, answers, asked, failedRedo, findings (claimed and kept tier, source), unknowns, unlisted, failedLenses, failedCritics, issues, revised, addedAssumptions and written, whose previousSha256 is the baseline out was checked against.

Roles: Extractor (Scribe tier), Writer (Planner tier, for the upstream's high-effort draft and revision) and Critic (Skeptic tier at high effort) are all std.claude.Text. Code writes out, not the reviser.

research-synthesis.summary: Sweep three web modalities, plus the repository on a pinned snapshot when a local context is given, for leads; deduplicate and rank them in code within code-owned territories; send each read and hunt to a web or local role by that territory; synthesize an answer whose citations code checks; and run one round of hunts for the gaps a tool-less critic finds, with confidence and status computed in code on every return path.
research-synthesis.preserved: Several parts of the upstream remain: the leads-then-reads split, the four modality charters with their named blind spots, ref normalization (lowercase, no trailing slash), the primary/secondary/anecdotal order of the ranking, the quick/standard/deep read caps (4/8/14), per-claim citations, a synthesis that keeps disagreements visible, a high-effort critic on the synthesizer's harness, exactly one extra round of at most three hunts, a revised synthesis only when a hunt found something, and the confidence thresholds (three primary sources and at most one gap for high, four sources for moderate). Batch 01's choice to rank missing credibility last is no longer needed because credibility is now required.
changes: Packaged: workflows/research-synthesis.ts holds only the control flow. contracts.ts has the lead, reading, hunt, critique and output schemas, the answer caps and the repository-relative Path contract. lib/policy.ts has the modality choice, the territory-keyed merge, rank, caps, hunt routing, source keys, the hunt fold, the citation check, and confidence and status, which conclude() derives on every return path. lib/snapshot.ts pins HEAD with a settled Git probe and refuses a local call that changed its snapshot or named a ref that is not a repository Path. Five templates and six fragments under prompts/ hold the prose.

No role holds both the repository's file tools and a web channel. Scout, Reader and Hunter have only WebSearch and WebFetch (std.claude.ReadOnly with its tools replaced). LocalScout, LocalReader and LocalHunter keep the file tools, have no web tools, and each runs in its own worktree of the commit pinned at the start, so localCommit is what they read even in a dirty checkout. The territory is code's, not the agent's: a lead from the local sweep is local whatever kind the scout gave it, and a lead from a web scout is web even when labelled local-code. The merge, the read routing, the hunts' known lists and the fold all key on it, and the prompts mark local sources as from this repository. The Synthesizer (Planner) and the Critic (Skeptic, effort high) are tool-less std.claude.Text roles. The critic first ran on Codex, but std.codex.Text reads through a sandbox that Codex lets read the whole disk, and it degraded every run on a Claude-only machine. The split is per call: both tool-less roles see local findings, and the Critic's hunt instructions reach the web Hunter, so only a prompt rule keeps local content out of a web hunt. The operator's context reaches every role. The upstream's low effort is the Copyist tier, its unspecified hunt effort Scribe.

Sweeps, deep reads and hunts are settled ctx.map calls (onError: 'return', versions sweep/1, read/1 and hunt/1, the sweeps keyed by modality) rather than tolerantPanel, because each answer must stay with its modality, lead or gap. Each failure is kept beside its item and counted: unswept modalities, unread leads (failed or not-useful), and per-gap hunt outcomes (found, empty, failed, or unhunted past the cap of three). Deferred leads are listed. A failed critic is recorded as critic: failed, and the draft stands. Any failure or unsearched territory makes the status degraded, the early returns included, so a run that could not search or read never reports no-leads or no-findings. A refused local call (a changed snapshot, or a ref outside the repository) fails its sweep, read or hunt rather than dropping one lead. The prompts state the schema caps (20 leads per sweep, 20 findings per reading, 10 gaps) and the path rule. An empty hunt reports source: null, and a useful hunt with no source fails validation.

Code owns the citations. Sources get keys S1, S2 and so on, and the synthesizer may cite only those keys. Code reports unknown and uncited keys, tells the critic which of the draft's keys match no source, and appends the key-to-ref list. Code also decides adequacy: an empty gap list. Confidence keeps the upstream thresholds but counts distinct sources that yielded findings, from deep reads and hunts alike, where upstream counted queued primary leads. It cannot be high after a failed critic, which upstream allowed. An answer that cites nothing, or cites an unknown key, is low and degraded. A reading marked useful with no findings now counts as not-useful, where upstream kept it. Ref normalization also trims whitespace, and a web ref never merges with a repository file of the same name. Ranking adds a within-tier tie-break that puts a lead several modalities found first, which can change which leads are read.

Interface: the schema requires question, so the upstream's error return is gone. context is nullable and enables the local sweep, which needs a Git repository with a commit. Elsewhere the settled probe fails, the context only grounds the prompts, and local is reported unswept (degraded) rather than the run failing. depth is an enum. The output adds status (answered, degraded, no-leads, no-findings), keyed sources with their territory and findings, tracked gaps with territories, critic, swept and unswept modalities, deferred leads with their territory, unread leads, citation checks and localCommit. answer is null instead of a stock sentence when nothing was found, and with no useful reading the run stops before synthesis.
research-synthesis.evaluation: The success fixture leaves an uncommitted edit in the checkout. Four sweeps return six distinct leads, the docs twice under different spellings. The checks assert the merge, both modalities on the docs, the top four read, two deferred and one reading not useful. The local lead's finding quotes the committed file, not the edit. The local sweep, local read and local hunt each ran in a snapshot pinned at HEAD; every other call had only web tools or no tools, all on Claude. The critic's prompt lists every source key, marks the local one as from this repository, and names the draft's unknown key S7 and the deferred leads. Of the four gaps, two web hunts add S4 and fold a reread into S1 with its contradiction, the local hunt comes back empty, and the fourth is unhunted; the revision prompt names each outcome. Nineteen modes each change one thing. no-context: a lead found by two modalities overtakes a single-modality one, and four primary sources give high confidence. standard-depth and deep-depth: 8 and 14 reads. no-leads and no-findings: clean empty statuses. all-sweeps-fail and all-reads-fail: degraded, not empty. Single failures: a web sweep (named to the critic), a read, the critic (moderate, not high) or a hunt. reader-changed, snapshot-changed and escaping-local: each local role that writes to its snapshot, or names a path outside the repository, is refused, and its write stays out of the checkout. mislabeled-local and mislabeled-web: a repository file labelled as docs is still read locally and never reaches a web prompt, while web leads labelled local-code go to web readers, never merge with the local lead, and a web hunt naming that path adds a web source. no-repository: local is unswept and every hunt is routed to the web. unknown-citation and uncited: degraded and low. In mutation runs, each of these failed a check: routing or the known lists keyed on kind, merge or fold ignoring territory, dropping either path check or the snapshot check, a critic with file tools or at medium effort, an unmarked local source, and each verdict or confidence clause. F3 does not apply because the port is read-only. The fixtures prove the routing, accounting, ranking and citation bookkeeping. They do not prove that real web research is accurate, that a cited key supports its claim, that the critic labels territories well or keeps local content out of web hunt instructions (only a prompt rule does that), or that restricted Claude's documented confinement of file tools to the working directory holds.

roadmap-plan.summary: Read the spec in code, decompose it into a capability graph that its schema holds numbered and acyclic, sequence it under three strategies as a settled map whose plans the schemas check against the graph, score the survivors, stress-test the winner against a code-computed critical path, and have a finalizer resolve every problem before code renders the roadmap and creates the document.
roadmap-plan.preserved: The upstream's capability decomposition (size, hard dependencies, technical risk separate from value), its three sequencing philosophies in their own words, the scored panel pick with one graft from a losing strategy, the five stress-test failure kinds with a concrete fix each, the milestone table with goals and exit gates, the called-out critical path and the risk register all remain, as do the spec/horizon/priorities/out inputs and the milestones/criticalPath/risks/strategy/roadmap outputs. Batch 01's labels survive as step IDs: decompose, strategies/<strategy>/plan, panel, critic and finalize.
changes: Packaged: workflows/roadmap-plan.ts is control flow only; contracts.ts holds the input and output and the decomposition, plan, pick and revision schemas built from the capabilities and surviving strategies, lib/graph.ts the numbering, cycle, placement, score and resolution rules plus the critical path, lib/policy.ts the strategy accounting, risk register and status, lib/render.ts the document, lib/spec.ts the spec read, and five templates with four fragments under prompts/ the prose.

Code owns the graph: a cyclic or dangling decomposition, a plan that schedules a capability before its dependency, misses or repeats one, or relies on a deferred one, and a judge whose winner lacks the top score are schema failures retried once. The critical path is the longest chain by size points (S 1, M 2, L 3, XL 5), computed in code and handed to the critic and finalizer instead of being named by the critic; the risk register is derived from the final plan.

The strategists are a settled ctx.map keyed by strategy, so a failed or refused plan is reported in failedStrategies with its kind and message and status turns degraded (no-strategy when none survive); a sole survivor skips the panel rather than being scored alone. Upstream's silent fallback to the first strategy and its null-tolerant critic are gone: a failed judge, critic or finalizer fails the run and resume retries it.

The finalizer returns the revised plan as data, not markdown: milestones with key risks, a deferred list (the value-first 'cut scope'), a resolution (applied or declined, with a note) for every numbered problem and an answer to the graft, so the output milestones are the committed roadmap rather than the winner's unrevised plan. Code renders the document and creates out exclusively instead of asking the agent to write it.

Every role is std.claude.Text (code reads the spec and writes the file) at the upstream's high effort: Planner tier for the decomposer, strategists and finalizer, Skeptic tier at high effort for the judge and critic, all borrowing ReadOnly's spend and time limits. Capability summaries and names reach the judge and critic, which upstream showed only capability ids; the critic also sees the spec to hunt hidden dependencies.
roadmap-plan.evaluation: The success fixture decomposes a five-capability notes spec, asserts the code-computed critical path C1 -> C2 -> C3 (7 points) in the critic's prompt and the output, the judge's value-first pick and de-risk-first graft, one applied and one declined resolution, the risk register from the final plan, byte-exact creation of docs/roadmap.md and that no call had a tool. Modes cover a failed strategist (degraded, two-way panel, sound plan), a sole survivor after code refuses a dependency-violating plan on both attempts (no panel, no graft), no surviving strategy (nothing written), an empty inline spec, an existing out (the run fails at the write with every agent step completed; a manual resume after freeing the path paid nothing again) and a cyclic decomposition refused before any strategist. F3 kills after the write and before its checkpoint. The fixtures prove the graph checks, accounting and publication, not the quality of a real decomposition or plan; the revised plan is not stress-tested again, as the document says.

sdlc-orchestrator.summary: Tailor a lifecycle and run every stage as a typed inline child under one run ID, composing the bootstrap and release-notes packages, with a durable review per stage that a decider may answer when autoApprove is set.
sdlc-orchestrator.preserved: Batch 02's tailored plan, typed children, stage-local redo answers, release gate before release notes and bounded redo remain, with the same frame and question IDs.
changes: One package, four workflows: the orchestrator and its document, implementation and verification stages, each runnable alone with --workflow. Bootstrap and release notes are the sibling packages' workflows, imported and declared as children, so their prompt roots join the static tree's fingerprint.

Each child's roster is its own; options.profiles maps child entries onto the orchestrator's Reader and Writer delegation ceilings, so under --require-grants one --grant Writer covers the setters and the implementer, and a launch without it is refused before any call.

autoApprove returns (Batch 02 dropped it) as a decide-then-act screen: when set and a stage's own gate passed, the Gatekeeper roster decider answers a choice question; only a confident continue skips the human review, and a low-confidence answer, a review answer or a failed screen still asks. Unlike upstream, a concerns gate always reaches the human.
Stage records note whether a human or the decider reviewed them.
sdlc-orchestrator.evaluation: Fixtures check one run ID, redo answers placed only in the requesting stage, the ten-stage lifecycle with approved bootstrap, implementation, QA, release gate and release publication on a clean checkout, the same lifecycle under requireGrants with and without the Writer grant, CLI exit 75 then answer and resume, and two CLI autoApprove runs (a confident decider skips both reviews; low confidence on spec asks the human). The decider runs from fixture answers; no live decision host is contacted, and a live run needs one configured. No content-quality equivalence is claimed.

security-audit.summary: Pin a revision, map its attack surface in a read-only snapshot, run each lens as a pipeline item that sweeps, drops findings whose file or line is absent and sends the rest straight to a severity-sized skeptic panel, and report only majority-upheld findings.
security-audit.preserved: The upstream's recon-then-sweep structure, its six lens charters and optional lens subset, the pipeline with no barrier and no cross-lens dedup between sweep and refutation, three seats for critical and high claims against one for medium and low, the floor(n/2)+1 majority, the refute-when-unreachable default, the severity-sorted report and the code-written summary when nothing survives all remain, as in Batch 01.
changes: Packaged: workflows/security-audit.ts is control flow only; contracts.ts holds the surface, finding, verdict and output schemas, lib/git.ts pins the revision and looks up cited files, lib/policy.ts the location rule, per-lens cap, panel sizes, majority, tally and plain report, and four templates with three shared fragments (snapshot, evidence-not-instructions, defensive scope) the prose.

Every reader works in its own snapshot of the pinned revision, started at the checkout root even when the run starts in a subdirectory, and a receipt check refuses one that changed it. Code looks up each lens's cited files at the revision (cat-file --batch-check, grep --count) and dismisses a missing file, a directory or a line past the end as unlocated before any seat is paid; located findings past maxFindingsPerLens, most severe first, are reported as unchecked.

The lens pipeline is a settled ctx.map, so a failed sweep is a failedLenses entry rather than a crash. Each finding's seats are their own settled map (tolerantPanel cannot pass a worktree); a failed seat stays in the arithmetic, so a finding that could still reach a majority is undecided rather than refuted, as upstream counted it. A recon failure fails the run for resume instead of returning an aborted result.

Inputs: lenses is a validated enum list run once each in a fixed order (upstream silently dropped unknown keys); revision, maxFindingsPerLens and crossHarness are new, the last seating CodexSkeptic second in every three-seat panel. The output keeps the whole surface map and adds status, revision, failedLenses and the refuted, undecided, unlocated and unchecked lists; upheld is a count beside seats, not upstream's 'n/m' string.

Roles: Mapper and Auditor are the Scribe tier (upstream set no effort), Skeptic the Skeptic tier at the upstream's high effort, Reporter the Copyist tier with no tools (its low effort). The reporter sees the confirmed findings, the undecided ones to list as unverified, and the gaps, never a refuted claim.
security-audit.evaluation: The success fixture checks the pinned revision, a critical and a high claim upheld by three-seat panels (3 of 3, 2 of 3), a medium refuted by its single seat, a low upheld, three code dismissals (missing file, directory, line past the end) that never reach a seat, severity order, a reporter that sees only survivors, every reader in an unchanged snapshot of the head, and a clean checkout with one pinned ref per snapshot call. Modes cover a failed seat (undecided, degraded, listed for manual review), a failed sweep (failedLenses), the per-lens cap (limited), Codex seats under crossHarness, all refuted and no findings (code-written reports, no reporter call), a run from a subdirectory (readers still start at the root) and an unknown revision refused before any call. Verdicts are scripted: nothing here shows that real auditors find, or skeptics correctly refute, real vulnerabilities, and confirmed findings remain agent claims, not certified vulnerabilities.

test-gap-filler.summary: Find and rank high-risk test gaps in an operator-selected source file, then propose a test and mutants; code owns the guarded test write, the baseline verdict and every mutation, including restoration after an interrupted attempt.
test-gap-filler.preserved: Batch 02's interface, serial mutation of one target, settled baseline and the mutation worker's reconcile-then-mutate-then-restore contract are unchanged, with the same step IDs (mutants/<id>/check).
changes: Packaged: the mutation worker is a real file, resources/mutation-worker.mjs, instead of a String.raw literal. lib/mutation.ts reads it when the module loads and passes its text with node -e, so the text stays part of every check's command identity, and the file is also in the package fingerprint.

The coverage and risk lenses get the upstream's distinct charters in one template; the Ranker has no tools and is the Planner tier (the upstream's high-effort rank), and the TestAuthor is read-only at the Mechanic tier.
Pure rules (unique gaps, single-anchor mutants) are in lib/mutation.ts; the workflow module keeps only the sequence.
test-gap-filler.evaluation: F3 kills the owner while a child test runs against mutated bytes, then resumes with orphan cleanup and verifies byte-identical pristine content. Settled baseline failures (nonzero exit, signal, timeout), surviving mutants and an unknown external edit (refused, then restored by the operator) are covered as in Batch 02. Test effectiveness beyond the fixture is not established.
